briefs.title: Fine particles outdoors
briefs.fact: WHO estimated 4.2 million premature deaths worldwide from outdoor air pollution in 2019; this is a modeled population burden.
briefs.pathway: Fine airborne particles are inhaled from varied sources such as fires, transport, industry and combustion.
briefs.check: Use air-quality monitoring, daily advisories and wildfire-smoke alerts where available. U.S. readers can consult AirNow.
briefs.boundary: A global burden estimate or local monitor does not identify the responsible source of an individual's illness.

briefs.title: Polluting household cooking fuels
briefs.fact: WHO reported about 2.1 billion people worldwide cook using polluting fuels or technologies in its December 2025 fact sheet.
briefs.pathway: Burning wood, coal, kerosene or other polluting fuels indoors can create harmful airborne particles.
briefs.check: Look for public programs supporting cleaner cooking fuels and technologies; ventilation alone may not eliminate the exposure.
briefs.boundary: This global household-energy estimate does not assess the air quality or choices available in any particular home.

briefs.title: Lead in drinking water
briefs.fact: WHO states that no level of lead exposure is known to be without harmful effects; young children are especially vulnerable.
briefs.pathway: Lead can leach from service lines, solder and plumbing; exposure also occurs through dust, paint and industrial sources.
briefs.check: Ask your water provider for its annual quality report, learn about the service line, and arrange appropriate tap testing when concerned. Boiling does not remove lead.
briefs.boundary: A utility report or a home's age does not tell you the lead concentration at a particular tap.
sources: Sources of lead in drinking water

briefs.title: PFAS in water and food
briefs.fact: NIH reviews associations between exposure to certain PFAS and immune, cholesterol, reproductive and other effects; evidence differs among chemicals.
briefs.pathway: Some PFAS can reach people through drinking water, food and occupational or product-related routes.
briefs.check: Ask which specific PFAS were tested in your water, seek a qualified laboratory for private wells, and consult local guidance on appropriate treatment.
briefs.boundary: A positive test does not itself establish a health effect or identify a legally responsible company. PFAS chemicals are not interchangeable.

briefs.title: Arsenic in groundwater
briefs.fact: WHO identifies long-term inorganic arsenic exposure through drinking water as a cause of cancer and other harmful outcomes.
briefs.pathway: Natural geology can introduce arsenic into aquifers used for drinking, cooking and irrigation.
briefs.check: For private wells, ask local public-health or groundwater authorities whether arsenic testing is indicated, and use a qualified laboratory.
briefs.boundary: A regional groundwater map cannot establish the quality of an individual well. Water can look normal while containing contaminants.

briefs.title: Methylmercury in fish
briefs.fact: WHO identifies methylmercury as a concern for fetal and early-childhood neurological development; some fish accumulate more than others.
briefs.pathway: Mercury can transform in aquatic ecosystems, build up in fish and reach people through seafood.
briefs.check: Consult local fish-consumption advisories for local catches. FDA/EPA guidance helps people who are pregnant and children choose lower-mercury fish.
briefs.boundary: Risk depends on species, location and consumption. This is not a reason to reject all nutritious fish or accuse one producer.

briefs.title: Electronic waste and unsafe recycling
briefs.fact: WHO reports 62 million tonnes of e-waste generated globally in 2022; just 22.3% was documented as formally collected and recycled.
briefs.pathway: Unsafe burning, dismantling and dumping can expose workers and communities to hazardous air, dust, soil and water mixtures.
briefs.check: Use authorized electronics recycling and take-back programs where available. Support safer collection and protections for informal workers.
briefs.boundary: The global waste figure does not prove contamination or illness in any particular neighborhood.
sources: Electronic waste: digital dumpsites and children

briefs.title: Radon inside buildings
briefs.fact: U.S. EPA identifies radon as a naturally occurring radioactive gas that can cause lung cancer; it cannot be seen or smelled.
briefs.pathway: Radon can enter buildings from soil and accumulate indoors; actual concentration differs by building.
briefs.check: Test indoor radon with an appropriate kit or qualified professional and follow local agency advice about mitigation if levels are elevated.
briefs.boundary: A regional risk map does not tell you the radon level in a specific home. Testing does not attribute an individual cancer case.

briefs.title: Heat and preventable illness
briefs.fact: CDC describes heat exhaustion, heat stroke and other heat-related illness risks, with greater danger in certain health and working conditions.
briefs.pathway: Indoor or outdoor heat, physical activity and barriers to cooling can overwhelm the body's temperature control.
briefs.check: Follow local heat alerts; identify accessible cooling, water and rest. Suspected heat stroke requires emergency help.
briefs.boundary: A regional forecast is not an individual medical assessment. Cooling access and working conditions change exposure.

briefs.title: Respirable silica at work
briefs.fact: CDC/NIOSH warns that breathing respirable crystalline silica during certain jobs can lead to silicosis and other serious diseases.
briefs.pathway: Cutting, drilling, grinding and polishing some stone and other materials can produce fine respirable silica dust.
briefs.check: Workers and employers should assess task-specific exposure, use effective engineering controls and follow applicable occupational-health requirements.
briefs.boundary: A job title or material alone does not measure dose. Occupational exposure needs appropriate assessment.
